title: MercadoLibre's Rescued Round and the Plan to Make It Last
dek: In 2000 a funding round nearly collapsed with the Nasdaq, and MercadoLibre's founders halved the staff to make the money last through the crashes that followed.

story.event: Closing a near-failed round as the Nasdaq fell, then halving staff to make the money last
story.summary: In March 2000 MercadoLibre, launched in Buenos Aires in 1999, had about 200 staff, a free service and debts, when investors in its second round pulled out as the Nasdaq fell; pressure from an existing investor kept the round of about $46 million alive and the money arrived in May 2000. Marcos Galperin and Hernán Kazah then cut staff from about 200 to 100, dropped costly advertising and set out to make the money last. The company survived the dot-com bust and Argentina's 2001 to 2002 crisis, took eBay on as a 19.5 per cent shareholder in 2001, first made a net profit in 2005 and listed on the Nasdaq in 2007.
paragraphs: MercadoLibre went live in August 1999 from a garage in Saavedra, a Buenos Aires neighbourhood. Two of its founders, Marcos Galperin and Hernán Kazah, had met as MBA students at Stanford, and the auction site soon ran in several Latin American countries. By March 2000 it had about 200 employees and a free service that earned nothing, and it had spent more than the $7.6 million raised in October 1999. It was running on debt, and its second round was due to close.

That month the Nasdaq began to fall. One by one, Kazah later recalled, interested investors rang to withdraw, until Goldman Sachs, which was leading the round, said it would not invest either. The founders thought the company would shut. Susan Segal, then running Chase Capital, an existing investor, pressed Goldman to stay in, and a round of about $46 million closed; the money reached the bank in May 2000. "It was a miracle," Kazah said. Galperin has called the bursting of the bubble one of the hardest obstacles the company faced, because it shut off access to capital.

The near-miss changed how they treated the money. Internet use in the region was tiny, and nobody knew when investors would return. They chose to make the round last for years. If the company still failed, Kazah said, it would fade, but "we're not going to put ourselves between a rock and a hard place just because of overspending." They cut the staff from about 200 to 100, pulled teams spread across countries into one, stopped expensive advertising and bought cheap search traffic instead. "We really saved the money for the rainy days," Galperin said in 2011.

The rainy days came. In September 2001 eBay swapped its Brazilian subsidiary for 19.5 per cent of MercadoLibre. When Argentina's economy broke down in 2001 and 2002, with exchange controls and a devalued peso, traffic rose as people cut off from their savings sold their belongings on the site. Rivals, Galperin said, ran out of cash first. MercadoLibre lost money every year until 2004, made a net profit of $2.4 million in 2005, and listed on the Nasdaq in August 2007.

quote.text: Profligacy consists not in spending years of time or chests of money,--but in spending them off the line of your career. The crime which bankrupts men and states, is, job-work;--declining from your main design, to serve a turn here or there.
quote.source_title: The Conduct of Life, Project Gutenberg eBook #39827
quote.connection: Emerson would not praise the cuts for their own sake. His test is direction: spending on the line of your work is safe, spending off it ruins. MercadoLibre kept paying for engineers and search traffic while it dropped offices and advertising, a harder judgement than simple thrift.

reflection: Kazah's line is worth keeping: if we fail after a long runway, so be it, but not because we overspent. It is a way of deciding in advance what kind of failure you could live with, and that decision is easier to make in a good month than a frightening one.

Your runway is not only money. It is energy, evenings, sleep and the goodwill of the people around you. Emerson's warning is not about spending them; it is about spending them off the line of your work: the meeting that serves nobody, the task taken on to please, the late night that only makes tomorrow harder.
invitation: Look at this week's calendar and find one commitment that sits off the line of your main work. Hand it on, shrink it to fifteen minutes, or let it go.

sources.supports: Kazah and Galperin met at Stanford; quick expansion to several countries; first round of $7.6 million closed in October 1999, led by Chase Capital Partners; about 200 employees and more than $7.6 million spent by March 2000, running on debt; investors withdrawing as the Nasdaq fell; Goldman Sachs, leading the round, declining to invest; Susan Segal of Chase Capital pressing it to stay; the round of about $46 million closing, 'a miracle', with the money arriving in May 2000; the service still free; the decision to make the money last and 'we're not going to put ourselves between a rock and a hard place just because of overspending'; staff reduced from 200 to 100, teams consolidated, marketing moved to Google search traffic, SEO and affiliates; eBay becoming an almost 20% shareholder; listing in August 2007.

sources.title: Marcos Galperin: Growing Latin America's Online Marketplace
sources.publisher: Stanford Graduate School of Business, Insights (Michele Chandler, 1 March 2011)
sources.supports: Galperin, MBA '99, founded the company after Stanford; spending little on expensive advertising in the early 2000s; 'We really saved the money for the rainy days'; competitors running out of cash while MercadoLibre still had money in the bank; traffic rising during the 2001-2002 Argentine crisis as people who had lost access to their savings sold their assets; eBay's stake in 2001; break-even in 2005; 2007 Nasdaq listing.

cross_checks.claim: As the Nasdaq fell in early 2000, MercadoLibre's second round nearly collapsed but closed at about $46 million.
The bursting of the bubble in March 2000 cut off MercadoLibre's access to capital.
MercadoLibre was started in 1999 in Buenos Aires by Galperin, Kazah and others.
After the round the company spent frugally, cutting advertising and saving its cash.
In September 2001 eBay took 19.5% of MercadoLibre in exchange for its Brazilian iBazar subsidiary.
MercadoLibre lost money until 2004 and first made a net profit (or broke even) in 2005.
Argentina's 2001-2002 crisis brought exchange controls and devaluation, and MercadoLibre's traffic rose during it.

research_notes: The slate dated the episode 2001; the documented decision came in spring 2000, when the second round nearly failed as the Nasdaq fell, and the story follows its consequences through 2001-2002. The account of the round and the cuts rests mainly on co-founder Hernán Kazah's 2025 podcast interview (show transcript on Buzzsprout, likely machine-generated); Infobae (2021) corroborates the round, its timing and its size from an earlier Kazah interview, and Galperin's 2019 remarks (iProUP) confirm that the March 2000 crash shut off capital. Galperin is not on record, in sources found, describing the 200-to-100 cut; it is attributed to the company's choices as Kazah told them. Round size: Kazah says 'like $46 million' (2025) and $46.5 million (Infobae 2021); the story says about $46 million. Timing of the close: Kazah says the money arrived in May 2000; one secondary source (not cited) dates the close to November 2000; the story uses Kazah. Cash figures conflict and are kept out of the story: Galperin told Stanford GSB (2011) 'when our competitors ran out of cash, we still had $40 million in the bank'; Kazah (2025) said that 'into the bag' they received probably less than 40% of the round because of the debt, and that about a quarter of the round was still in the bank at the 2007 IPO. The story quotes only 'saved the money for the rainy days' and that rivals ran out of cash first. eBay stake: 19.5% in eBay's 2001 10-K and the 2001 report; Stanford GSB and Kazah say 20% or 'almost 20%'; the story uses 19.5%. Profitability: the 2007 prospectus says net income was negative from 1999 until 2004 and positive from 2005 ($2.4 million); Stanford GSB says break-even in 2005; Kazah recalls being profitable at the end of 2006; a secondary summary of an Endeavor interview has Galperin saying the company made its first profit in 2007. The story uses the prospectus figures. Galperin's quotation in Spanish (iProUP) is paraphrased rather than translated inside quotation marks. Several Argentine profiles say the company nearly closed in 2001; the founders' own accounts place the near-death moment in March-May 2000, which the story follows.
